# Run onError and afterSession when beforeSession throws

Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#94
Labels: priority:medium, type:bug, size:S, area:api

## Why

`beforeSession` is awaited before the `try` block opens, so a throw from it escapes before the `catch` and `finally` exist. Neither `onError` nor `afterSession` runs.

That breaks the guarantee the hook names imply. A deployer who allocates something in `beforeSession` — a span, a database handle, a rate-limit token — and releases it in `afterSession` leaks it on exactly the path where the allocation failed, and learns nothing from `onError` because it never fires. The failure is silent in the engine and visible only as an unexplained rejection at the caller.

Recorded as measured behaviour in `specs/hal-engine-config-hooks/spec.md` by HALEngine#83, which scoped itself to specifying the seam rather than changing it, and raised again by the reviewer on that PR. The spec notes this property is owned by no issue in the epic; this is that issue.

## What to do

Move the `beforeSession` call inside the `try`, so a throw from it reaches the same `catch` and `finally` as any other failure in the turn, and decide one question explicitly: whether `afterSession` running after a failed `beforeSession` is what a deployer wants, or whether it needs to know the session never started. Record the answer in the spec either way, because a cleanup hook that cannot tell "never allocated" from "allocated and finished" is a new trap for the same reader.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `beforeSession` that throws still reaches the caller as a rejection, unchanged from today
- [ ] `onError` fires for that throw, with the same argument shape as any other orchestrator failure
- [ ] `afterSession` fires for that throw, and the spec states what a hook can assume about how much of the turn happened
- [ ] A non-throwing `beforeSession` behaves exactly as today, pinned by the existing tests remaining unedited
- [ ] `specs/hal-engine-config-hooks/spec.md` replaces its recorded-flaw line with the new guarantee, and the CHANGELOG says what changes for an existing consumer
- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`) and `npm run prettier:check` pass

## Tech notes

Key files: `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` (the `beforeSession` call above the `try`), `specs/hal-engine-config-hooks/spec.md`.

Out of scope: the `instanceof Error` gate on `onError` (its own issue) and usage accounting across tool rounds (HALEngine#93).

<section name="Conventions" source="repo" priority="1">
<document source="AGENTS.md" type="doc" relevance="0.98" tokens="737">
## Spec Test Links

Statements in `specs/*/spec.md` cite their validating test in a trailing
parenthetical at the end of the statement, where a list item counts as one
statement and a paragraph counts per sentence. Tests live beside their source
in this repo, so the path points into `src/`:

```markdown
- All entries within a single assistant response are committed before the next
  user message is processed
  ([validated by: commits every entry before the next user message](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.test.ts#L42)).
```

The citation carries the test's **name** as well as its line. The name is what the
author cited; the line is a derived pointer, and it goes stale on its own - adding
an import above a suite moves every test below it, and the citation lands on a
different, still-valid declaration without anything noticing. `npm run spec:names`
holds each citation to the test it names, and `npm run spec:names:fix` repoints the
line from the name. The `#Lnn` stays because the lint rule and the coverage job
both index by it; a citation without one marks the whole file covered rather than
one test.

A citation counts as coverage only where it is trailing, and a test link placed
anywhere else in the statement is a misplaced citation rather than a weaker one.
Upstream `check:spec-links` reports it and exits 1, and the coverage job that
consumes these specs records nothing for it - so a spec can read as fully cited while its coverage is
zero. A mid-statement link to something that is not a test file - a script, a
doc, another spec - is ordinary prose, is never reported, and was never coverage
to begin with. A misplaced citation is fixed by moving it to the end of its
statement, never by deleting it.

In a test file the `#Lnn` anchor must land on the `it(`, `test(` or `describe(`
declaration itself - not a blank line, not one holding only closing punctuation,
and not a line inside the test body. A citation onto an `expect` renders and
resolves like any other, and proves nothing: no reader can turn that line back
into the name of a case. `scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` reports all four as
`rotten` and exits 1 in both modes. A citation into a file that is not a test -
a workflow, a config, `package.json` - has no declaration to land on and is held
only to existing and carrying content.

What no gate can catch is an anchor aimed at the wrong declaration: a real but
unintended `it(` passes every check. The tell is that the test the statement
meant to cite goes on reading as uncited in the `require-spec-link` backlog.

Anchors drift silently whenever a cited file gains or loses lines above them, so
after editing any cited file re-run `node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs`
rather than hand-correcting the numbers. That script cannot repair a spec absent
from the base ref, since it has no baseline to translate from; on the branch that
introduces a spec, its anchors have to be corrected by hand.
</document>
<document source="specs/hal-engine-spec-anchor-drift/spec.md" type="spec" relevance="0.52" tokens="852" truncated="true">
## Rotten anchors

Independent of any baseline, an anchor must land somewhere real. Four ways it does not, all reported as `rotten` and all failing the run in both modes:

- the cited file does not exist in the working tree ([validated by: reports a citation into a file that is not in the working tree](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L291)).
- the line is past the end of the file ([validated by: reports an anchor past the end of the cited file](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L299)).
- the line is blank, or holds only closing punctuation — `)`, `]`, `}`, `>`, `,`, `;` ([validated by: fails in both modes when the anchor lands on a blank line](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L263), [closing punctuation](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L279)).
- the line is in a test file but is not the `it`/`test`/`describe` declaration ([validated by: reports an anchor that lands inside the test body as rotten](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L551)).

A rotten href is reported rather than quietly synced: a short-form label whose href lands on a blank line leaves both modes failing with nothing rewritten, instead of the label being pulled into agreement with a broken target ([validated by: reports a label whose href is rotten rather than silently syncing it](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L435)).

The last two are the ones that matter in practice. A citation that slides onto the closing bracket of the block it meant to name still resolves and still renders; it just proves nothing. A citation that slides onto an `expect` inside the body is worse, because it reads as a precise reference to a line no reader can turn back into the name of a case.

The declaration check is narrow on purpose:

- The declaration itself passes, and so does the enclosing `describe` — citing a group is a legitimate reference ([validated by: accepts an anchor on the it declaration itself](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L533), [describe](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L542)).
- Modified forms are declarations too: `it.each`, `test.skip` and the `f`/`x` prefixes all pass ([validated by: accepts the modified forms of a declaration](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L573)).
- Only test files are held to it. A citation into a workflow, a config or `package.json` has no declaration to land on and is exempt ([validated by: holds only test files to the rule, so a non-declaration line elsewhere passes](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L600)).
- It fails the plain run as well as `--check`, and rewrites nothing ([validated by: fails a body-line anchor in rewrite mode too, and rewrites nothing](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L560)).
- It composes with repointing rather than replacing it: a test citation still moves from one declaration to another as lines shift above it ([validated by: repoints a test citation from one declaration to another as lines shift](../../scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.test.ts#L583)).

What it does not catch is a citation aimed at the wrong declaration. `#Lnn` on a real but unintended `it` passes every check here, because nothing mechanical relates a statement's prose to a test's name. That failure mode is a review concern, and the `require-spec-link` backlog is the instrument that surfaces it: the test the citation should have named goes on reading as uncited.
</document>
</section>
